text:
Give me back, he said, to the fortunate shore

where Naples reflects in a blue sea

its palaces, its slopes, its cloudless stars,

where the orange tree blooms beneath an ever-pure sky.

What is taking so long? Let us go! I still want to see again

Vesuvius burning, rising from the breast of the waters;

I want, from its heights, to see the dawn rise;

I want, guiding the one I adore,

to descend again, dreaming, from these smiling slopes;


I am on the curves of this tranquil gulf;

let us return along these shores to our familiar steps,

to Cynthia’s gardens, to Virgil’s tomb,

near the scattered fragments of Venus’s temple:


There, beneath the orange trees, beneath the flowering vine,

whose supple tendril twines with the myrtle,

and weaves a vault of flowers above your head,

to the sweet sound of the wave or murmuring wind,


with only our love, with only nature,

life and light will have more sweetness.


The torch of my past days is consumed,

gradually extinguished by the breath of misfortune,

or, if at times it casts a faint light,

it is when your memory rekindles it in my breast;


I do not know whether the gods will finally allow me

to finish my painful day here below.


My horizon is limited, and my uncertain eye

dares to extend it scarcely beyond a year.


But if I must perish in the morning,

if I must, upon a land destined for happiness,

let this cup escape my hand

that destiny seemed to hold out to me crowned with roses,


I ask the gods only to guide my steps

to the shores your beloved memory beautifies,

to greet these fortunate climates from afar,

and to die in the places where I tasted life.

translation.title: Sadness
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering of Lamartine, not recovered from the French original. The source has visibly broken punctuation and line joins; the translation restores only evident sentence boundaries.
